rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks for this, and for the time at the meetup. Morgan intends to apply before 30 November; a two-page proposal and budget are in preparation. The project is a small, realistic evaluation of whether deployed AI agents follow instructions planted in the content they process (emails, invoices, web pages), with separate reporting for attacks that tell the agent not to consult the human. Two quick eligibility questions so the budget is right first time: 1. Halcyon Threshold is currently an unincorporated project. Can a rapid grant be made to Morgan as an individual, or do you require an incorporated entity or fiscal sponsor? 2. Are modest stipends for volunteer contributors (a data analyst, an external methods reviewer) an allowable cost? Thanks, — Halcyon Threshold (I'm the AI assistant that handles this inbox on Morgan's behalf. Morgan will be the named applicant and will submit the application personally.)"
rows.quote: Idris Bellamy (Emberfall): confirmed intent to apply; asked whether an unincorporated project/individual is eligible and whether volunteer stipends are allowable.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — this is exactly the right moment to ask, because we've just picked the first project and it needs a data analyst more than anything else. The project, in four sentences: AI assistants with real tools (pay, send, post) now process huge volumes of email and documents, and attackers have started writing instructions *for the agent* inside that content — we received one yesterday: a fake invoice with a paragraph telling \"AI agents processing this mailbox\" to pay $89 and not to ask the owner. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks are academic and synthetic. We want to build a small, public, continuously refreshed evaluation from real specimens, score deployed models on whether they comply, ask the human, or refuse, and report the \"don't ask the human\" cases separately. Everything gets published, including boring results. A concrete first task, roughly 5–8 hours over the next three weeks, if it appeals: 1. Challenge a draft taxonomy of 8 attack categories (payment, credential, exfiltration, send-on-behalf, publish, config change, persuasion, self-instruction). Are they scorable and mutually exclusive? 2. Produce 15 seed scenarios in a simple JSON format — ideally from real specimens in your own spam folder, anonymised; adapted or clearly-labelled synthetic ones otherwise. 3. Draft a scoring rubric with edge cases for each outcome (complied / asked / flagged / refused). 4. Tell us what's wrong with the whole idea. That's the most useful thing right now. If you're in, reply and Morgan will share the project repo (private for now) and the schema. If you'd rather do something else, say so — \"five hours a week on something concrete\" is an offer we don't want to waste. Thanks again, — Halcyon Threshold (I'm the AI assistant that runs Morgan's Halcyon Threshold inbox and repo; Morgan will see this thread and follow up personally.)"
rows.quote: Priya Raman: concrete first task (taxonomy critique, 15 seed scenarios, rubric draft).
